perUnit.text: An assistant on a portfolio does harm the moment it guesses: someone asks about my work, gets a confident answer I never published, and leaves believing something about me that isn't true. So the assistant I built, Ask, answers only from what is published on milesroxas.com.

Press ⌘K anywhere on the site, or open the Ask tab in the dock, and ask about my work in plain words. The answer stays under 120 words and lists the pages it used. When the honest answer is "ask Miles", it says so and opens a short form that reaches me.

Much of Ask's design is about that last case: knowing when not to answer. I built it first for the Suits & Sandals site, then ported it here. This post covers the index Ask reads from, the path from question to answer, the judge that decides when a question comes to me, what that judge cost, and what Ask keeps. The judge has the clearest result: on the Suits & Sandals site, it raised the right handoff card from 52 to 57 of 57 test turns.

I build with AI coding agents. Across this repo, 261 of 486 commits carry an AI co-author line. On Ask, I designed how it behaves and directed the build, reviewing each change. [check: how design, direction, review and code were split on Ask, which nothing records]

Ask's index holds what an anonymous visitor can read, and nothing more. It is one table, `ask_embeddings`, in Postgres with pgvector, an extension that stores embeddings beside ordinary rows. The table is declared in Drizzle next to the schema of Payload, the CMS behind the site. Nothing outside the CMS writes to it.

Drafts and protected client work never reach it. The indexer reads each document the way an anonymous visitor would, so the site's own access rules do the filtering. A protected case study fails the read, and what fails the read can't be retrieved.

The index changes when a document is published or unpublished, not when it is saved. An `afterChange` hook on Pages, Works, Posts and Site Info re-embeds a document when it is published. Draft saves and autosave are skipped, and an unpublish deletes the document's rows. A half-written draft never reaches an answer, and taking a page down takes it out of Ask in the same step.

Ask looks for evidence before any model writes a word. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small turns the question into a 1,536-dimension vector; a follow-up is embedded alone and joined to the previous question. perUnit.text: In a small town, a local business's event usually ends up on a platform where ads, reviews and ranking algorithms decide what deserves attention. [check: where people in Buzlee's towns found events before, so this can name it] I worked with Buzlee's founder [check: name, and whether to credit them by name] to shape an MVP with none of the three, then designed and built the mobile apps and the systems behind them.
Buzlee is a digital bulletin board for small towns: one feed and one map for what is on this week, posted by local businesses and approved by a person.

The model for Buzlee already existed off the screen. A business pins a flyer to a bulletin board, anyone walking past can read it, and nothing decides that one flyer deserves more attention than another. Buzlee keeps those rules and puts the board on a phone.

A small town also has few enough events each week for a person to read every post before it goes up. That makes human approval workable here, where a larger platform would hand the job to software. [check: that this was the reasoning and whose it was (Miles's, the founder's or shared), and roughly how many posts arrive in a week]
The founder and I shaped the MVP around three decisions, and each one gave something up. [check: which of these were the founder's calls and which were Miles's]

**A person approves every post.** A flyer goes live only after someone reads it, rather than when an automated filter passes it. The cost is time: someone reviews every post, and a business waits before its event appears. [check: who approves posts and how long approval usually takes] **Nothing is ranked.** The feed and the map show what is on, and no algorithm pushes an event up for being popular. The cost is that Buzlee never learns what a person likes and shows them more of it. **No ads and no ratings.** A business can't pay to rise, and no event carries a score. That gives up advertising as a way to pay for the app.

I designed and built the mobile apps and the systems that support them. [check: which platforms, and what the supporting systems include, for example the posting tool for businesses and the approval queue] [check: who else worked on the build, including any AI-assisted development, so the split of the work can be stated here]

People find events two ways: a feed of what is on this week, and a map that places each event where it happens. Local businesses post their events as flyers. Each flyer reaches the feed and the map only after a person approves it.

Buzlee went from concept to working mobile apps and the systems that support them. [check: status (live in the app stores, in beta or in a pilot) and since when, which towns use it, and any number Miles can share, such as businesses posting or events listed]

Most of Buzlee's design is in what it refuses: ads, ratings and ranking. I would decide those refusals first again, before any feature. What I haven't settled is scale: a person can read every flyer in one small town, and I don't know yet whether that holds as Buzlee adds towns.
